items.titleEn: Blue Jays blanked by A's in crucial opportunity to gain AL Wild Card ground
bodyEn: WEST SACRAMENTO -- The Athletics team that the Blue Jays faced to begin their 2026 season on March 26 at Rogers Centre was hardly recognizable when the two clubs met up this week at Sutter Health Park.

The Athletics’ original Nos. 1-5 batters -- Nick Kurtz, Shea Langeliers, Tyler Soderstrom, Brent Rooker and Jacob Wilson -- are all on the injured list, as is Opening Day starting pitcher Luis Severino. And yet, Blue Jays manager John Schneider warned before Monday’s series opener, that the underperforming club could still be dangerous.
“They always play us tough,” Schneider said.

That was the case once again as the Blue Jays suffered a 2-0 shutout loss to the A’s on Wednesday, dropping two of three games in a crucial September series, and losing ground in the American League Wild Card race. At 73-74, Toronto fell to 1 1/2 games behind Cleveland for the final AL Wild Card spot, although the Blue Jays could pick up half a game if the Guardians fall to the Orioles on Wednesday evening.

After losing a three-game road set to the A’s in their first-ever series at Sutter Health Park last July, the Blue Jays were held to six hits by lefty Brady Basso and four relievers as their struggles in West Sacramento continued.

Their best chance came in the fifth inning when Vladimir Guerrero Jr. came up with men on first and third and one out, but he bounced into a 1-4-3 double play to end the threat. The A’s scored in the third and fourth innings of a bullpen game for Toronto, and that was enough.

The Blue Jays still finished their nine-game road trip that also featured road series against the Guardians and Royals with a 5-4 record, but they missed out on a golden opportunity to gain ground against an A’s team that came into Wednesday 30 games under .500.

items.titleEn: Okamoto hits 30th HR to propel Blue Jays in hunt for Wild Card spot
bodyEn: WEST SACRAMENTO -- In nearly every answer he gave after leading the Blue Jays to a 4-2 win over the Athletics on Tuesday at Sutter Health Park, Kazuma Okamoto’s message was clear: Toronto isn’t done yet.

While Okamoto acknowledged he met a personal goal by hitting his 30th home run of an impressive rookie season, he continued to point to what comes next: 16 crucial regular-season contests that will determine his club’s postseason fate. With Tuesday’s win, the Blue Jays (73-73) remain one game out of the final American League Wild Card spot.

“Definitely, it’s great to get to 30 in my first year, but we’ve still got a few games to go here,” Okamoto said through interpreter Yusuke Oshima. “I want to flip the switch and focus on the games moving forward.”

Okamoto is certainly flipping the switch in September, batting .333 (9-for-27) with a 1.009 OPS in seven games during the month. He followed up a 423-foot solo home run in Monday night’s 6-5 walk-off loss with another dinger on Tuesday, going back to back with Josh Smith to begin the second inning. He tied White Sox infielder Munetaka Murakami for the most home runs by AL rookies in 2026, just one behind Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart for the Major League lead.

With the solo blast to left off A’s starter Jack Perkins, Okamoto recorded the 10th season by a player born in Japan to reach the 30-homer plateau. Shohei Ohtani has done it six times, Murakami has done so in 2026, Seiya Suzuki hit 32 homers last season, and Hideki Matsui created the club with 31 dingers in 2004.
“It’s a pretty cool milestone, 30,” Blue Jays manager John Schneider said. “Pretty good list he just joined of Japanese players there.”

Maybe it’s unsurprising that Okamoto would slug 30 dingers in his first MLB season: He did so for six straight years, from 2018-23, with the Yomiuri Giants of Nippon Professional Baseball, racking up 248 career home runs in NPB.

Okamoto has struggled at times in the Majors -- including for much of the second half -- but his recent surge has been promising. Schneider pointed to the right-handed slugger’s final at-bat in the ninth inning, in which Okamoto wasn’t quite on a slider at the bottom of the zone but still drove it 310 feet to center at 94.3 mph.
“Kaz is swinging the bat well,” Schneider said. “Even the flyout to center on the breaking ball -- he’s kind of riding through some breaking balls, too, and really kind of squaring up the fastball.”

Okamoto’s hard work isn’t just in the batting cage, either. The infielder took the field early on Tuesday despite temperatures in the mid-90s in sunny West Sacramento, taking part in extra infield drills with third-base coach Carlos Febles.

On Tuesday, Okamoto’s glovework at the hot corner was considerably improved from a day earlier, when he committed two errors on the same rundown play in the first inning to bring in a run for the A’s.
“Mistakes happen, obviously,” Okamoto said. “I can’t change that, so all I can do is forget about it and focus on the next game and the next play.”

Okamoto couldn’t handle a pair of swinging bunts down the third-base line from A’s speedster Henry Bolte -- similar to the soft infield single from Max Muncy that kickstarted Monday’s A’s rally in the ninth -- but held his own at third. He made a nice backhanded stop on a grounder from Tommy White in the second inning, then ranged into foul ground to set his feet and throw out Alika Williams in the seventh.
“He works his tail off defensively,” Schneider said. “He’s turned into a pretty surehanded guy over there.”

It’s evident how much Okamoto wants to help the Blue Jays defend their 2025 AL pennant, and so far, he’s been perhaps their most productive hitter. Okamoto’s .762 OPS is tied with Alejandro Kirk for tops on the team among players with at least 100 plate appearances, and his 30 homers are far and away the most among Toronto hitters. George Springer is second with 14, and six-time All-Star Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has only eight.
That means it’s been Okamoto leading the charge, a role he seems to embrace even through the ups and downs he’s had throughout his standout rookie year.
“Right now, things are going well,” Okamoto said. “We only have a few more games here while we make a push for the postseason. Hopefully I can keep going.”

items.titleEn: Giménez, Blue Jays feel the whiplash of almost-comeback win
bodyEn: WEST SACRAMENTO -- Andrés Giménez stood in the batter’s box as if frozen in place, keeping his bat extended and watching his game-tying ninth-inning home run in flight. He posed there for several seconds before jogging down the first-base line and flipping his bat end over end in front of a raucous Blue Jays dugout.

Just twenty minutes later, Giménez crouched to the left of the mound, stunned into silence. His all-out effort to field a bases-loaded chopper from Athletics first baseman Jeff McNeil hadn’t quite been enough: McNeil beat the rap at first base for a walk-off infield hit in the bottom of the ninth.
In a matter of moments, Giménez and the Blue Jays had experienced all the ups and downs of high-stakes, high-tension September baseball in Monday’s 6-5 loss at Sutter Health Park.

Giménez’s homer in the ninth to fully erase Toronto’s early 5-1 deficit looked like it might spark a dramatic comeback win. Instead, it just made things all the more painful -- especially since the Blue Jays had a chance to sneak back into an American League Wild Card spot thanks to the Guardians’ 6-4 loss to the Orioles earlier in the day.
“We’ve got to shake this one off and come back tomorrow,” Blue Jays manager John Schneider said.

It might not be easy for Toronto to bounce back from a game in which its ace and its lockdown closer both stumbled. Starter Dylan Cease was tagged for five runs (four earned) in five innings, while closer Louis Varland -- pitching in a tie game in the ninth -- failed to send the game to extra innings.

Varland’s struggles, at least, are more attributable to poor luck than to total ineffectiveness. Donovan Walton and Henry Bolte both drew walks to end plate appearances that featured a number of borderline pitches called balls. The Blue Jays, who lost both of their ABS challenges by the fourth inning, were powerless to change the outcome.

The Athletics’ hits against Varland in the ninth were hardly scorchers. Max Muncy led off the decisive frame by reaching on a 42.7 mph tapper to third base, while McNeil’s walk-off hit was all of 51.9 mph off the bat. Only one ball in the inning -- a line drive to center field for the second out -- even left the infield.
“It’s going to happen sometimes,” Schneider said. “No one else I’d rather have out there than Louis. Good placement by them.”
Cease, meanwhile, continued his struggles at Sutter Health Park. He allowed a career-high nine earned runs in his only previous start in West Sacramento, back in April 2025 with the Padres.
The right-hander’s average four-seam fastball velocity on Monday was just 94.9 mph, more than 2 mph below his season average of 97.1, but Cease expressed little concern for the sizable dip.
“I think it’s just late in the season,” Cease said. “I’ve got to kind of roll with what I’ve got and figure out how I can maybe maximize it a little better.”

Among the least effective pitchers in MLB when it comes to controlling the running game, Cease was repeatedly victimized on the basepaths during Monday’s start. The A’s swiped five bases in the first three innings, including two apiece for Henry Bolte and Zack Gelof, which led to two runs against Cease in the third. That brought Cease’s total to an MLB-high 31 stolen bases allowed this season.
“I wish I had a little more focus on that,” Cease said of the Athletics’ disruptive baserunning. “I feel like looking back, I kind of just let it happen. They definitely took advantage.”

Technically, the Blue Jays did manage to catch a runner stealing home in the first inning, but they didn’t get the out they needed. With men on the corners, Carlos Cortes broke for second, and Toronto catcher Alejandro Kirk caught Gelof off third, but a missed catch and then a poor throw from third baseman Kazuma Okamoto -- who was charged with two errors on the play -- ruined the rundown and brought in a second A’s run.

“We talked about it before the game: Against a pitcher like [Cease], they’re going to take chances,” Schneider said. “We’ve got to do a better job of limiting those extra bases. First inning, really, too, we’ve got to handle the baseball.”

Okamoto atoned for the mistake with a home run to lead off the Blue Jays’ three-run seventh inning, and Giménez made up for a baserunning gaffe of his own to bring Toronto level in the ninth, but ultimately, it wasn’t enough.

items.titleEn: Santander (torn labrum) to begin Triple-A rehab assignment
bodyEn: WEST SACRAMENTO -- A big bat is nearing a return to the Blue Jays. But will he be back by the end of the regular season?

Anthony Santander is set to begin a rehab assignment on Wednesday with Triple-A Buffalo, manager John Schneider announced before Monday’s series opener against the Athletics at Sutter Health Park. After undergoing surgery to repair a torn left shoulder labrum in February, Santander will begin working his way back to the Major Leagues.

The outfielder will need a lengthy, Spring Training-style ramp-up before rejoining Toronto, Schneider said. He will play his first rehab game as a designated hitter before getting reps in the outfield.

“It’ll be a handful of games, at least,” Schneider said of the assignment length. “We want to see how he’s feeling, how he’s hitting the ball. We’ll definitely be in touch with him once he gets rolling.”

When healthy, Santander could be a huge addition as a switch-hitting slugger with prodigious power: He crushed 44 homers for the Orioles during an All-Star 2024 campaign. But after signing a five-year, $92.5 million deal with the Blue Jays in January 2025, Santander was plagued by the shoulder injury throughout his first season in Toronto. He played just 54 regular-season games and batted just .175 with six home runs. Santander was a non-factor in the postseason, too, homering just once and posting a .564 OPS before being replaced on the roster midway through the ALCS.
After seeing no game action since mid-October, Santander might be a bit rusty in his initial appearances for the Bisons, but the Blue Jays won’t be pushing the panic button.
“He’s notoriously kind of a slow starter, too, so we want to make sure that he’s functioning at the normal level that he can,” Schneider said. “If he can help us, it’d be great.”

While Santander’s career platoon splits are practically even -- he has a .767 career OPS against left-handed pitchers, compared to a .761 mark against righties -- he struggled considerably against southpaws in limited action with the Blue Jays in 2025. Santander went 7-for-48 (.146) with no homers, 20 strikeouts and a .442 OPS against lefties in 2025.

Still, Schneider said, Toronto wants Santander to focus more on getting healthy than fine-tuning his approach against left-handers. The club’s message as Santander prepares to begin his rehab assignment? “Go be you.”
“I know last year was a little different based on the shoulder and how he was feeling,” Schneider said. “It’s kind of like, ‘Go get ’em.’”

items.titleEn: 'Totally different' Blue Jays ready for final push toward playoffs
bodyEn: This story was excerpted from Keegan Matheson's Blue Jays Beat newsletter. To read the full newsletter, click here. And subscribe to get it regularly in your inbox.
KANSAS CITY -- It’s all sitting right in front of the Blue Jays now.

This season has been wildly imperfect, filled with more frustrating days than fun ones, but none of that matters now. The Blue Jays are back to .500 at 72-72, just one game out of the final AL Wild Card spot, and they hold the tiebreaker over the team they’re chasing, the Guardians.

This team is still scrambling, but so is everyone else. Spencer Arrighetti was hit hard in Sunday’s finale in Kansas City, and at this point, the Blue Jays only have three starters pitching well in Dylan Cease, José Soriano and Max Scherzer.

They’ve been finding ways to make it work, though, at least relative to the rest of the AL Wild Card race. These aren’t powerhouse teams, but someone needs to claim that third spot, and the Blue Jays still feel like a team with momentum.

“We’re just playing good ball. Everybody’s got a hand in this,” Scherzer said over the weekend. “Starters, relievers, hitters, defense, you name it. The catchers are doing great. It takes a team effort to get wins in the big leagues and that’s what we’re doing. You’re seeing guys up and down the roster contribute here, and across the organization, too. Pitchers are coming up and down, we’re dealing with pitching injuries left and right, but guys have come in and plugged a hole. When you get that as an organization, you asked why we’re winning? That’s why we’re winning.”

At this point, the Blue Jays have nothing to lose. If they take big risks and whiff, then so be it. There seems to be a freedom with this club now, particularly after the Trade Deadline shook up a group that had grown stagnant.

“It just feels like we're going out there and playing,” All-Star second baseman Ernie Clement said. “Nobody's stressed out. Nobody's worried about their own personal stats. Everybody's just going out there and playing and trying to win, and that's when we're at our best. We're worried about one thing and one thing only, and that's winning.”
Remaining schedulesBlue Jays: at A’s, vs. Tigers, vs. Orioles, at Rangers, at Orioles, vs. RedsGuardians: at Orioles, at Twins, vs. White Sox, vs. A’s, at Red Sox, at Royals

The Rangers are still a factor, too, just a game behind the Blue Jays and already holding the tiebreaker, so that series later in the month is crucial. Even if the Orioles fade, they also have six games left against the Blue Jays to shake things up. There won’t be anything simple about this.
These don’t feel like the Blue Jays of June and July, though.

They have Brett Bateman batting leadoff with a .347 average, delivering value on that Kevin Gausman trade well ahead of schedule. Charles McAdoo has a legitimate role now, and the veterans have picked up, including streaks from Alejandro Kirk and George Springer. If Vladimir Guerrero Jr. can turn his recent momentum into something bigger, that changes everything.

“It’s totally different,” John Schneider said. “Different music, different people, different feel. It’s always fun to come to the ballpark with this group, but it’s nice to win, it’s nice to get on a bit of a roll. … Right now, we come to the park expecting to win and we’re not really budging from that.”
Everyone’s been feeling this and talking about it, from the loudest voices on the team right down to the strong, silent types.

“We’ve been winning, so the vibes are good,” Kazuma Okamoto said through interpreter Yusuke Oshima. “Even when we’re losing, I think we’re doing a good job of just flipping the page and making sure that on the next day, it’s a new game and a new day. We’re just bringing a positive mindset and that has been helping.”

It also feels like there’s finally been a shift away from grasping at 2025 and that identity, which may have been an external narrative more than anything the Blue Jays, themselves, actually believed in. These aren’t the ‘25 Blue Jays, but this isn’t the ‘25 postseason race.

Sneaking in with the third Wild Card spot would likely line the Blue Jays up against either the Astros or the White Sox. Both are solid enough teams, but there are no giants waiting for the Blue Jays. This team doesn’t just have a shot to slip in, they have a shot to go on a run, and it’s all up to them in these final 18 games.

items.titleEn: Blue Jays unable to sweep, lose WC ground despite encouraging series
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- If the Blue Jays can reel off six more series like this to end the season, they’re headed to the postseason, but they couldn’t stick the landing for a sweep. ​

Sunday’s 6-1 loss to the Royals nudged the Blue Jays back to .500 and one game out of the final AL Wild Card spot, which now belongs to the Guardians again. The Blue Jays just beat those same Guardians and hold the season tiebreaker (4-2), but Cleveland has three walk-offs in their past three days.
This is what mattered most from Sunday in Kansas City:
1. Blue Jays still need more from Spencer Arrighetti
We can consider Arrighetti to be stretched all the way back out to a “starter” at this point, after throwing 91 pitches over 4 2/3 innings. Now, the Blue Jays need some quality out of those innings.

Arrighetti got rocked in the first, allowing a bunt single and walk to snowball when he served up a three-run shot to Vinnie Pasquantino. Salvador Perez later took him deep, too, and while Arrighetti allowed six runs, that number could have been even higher with all of the warning-track shots he gave up.

Better outings from Arrighetti aren’t a “want” for the Blue Jays, they’re a need. With Jameson Taillon back on the Blue Jays’ crowded IL, they’re stuck using a bullpen day as their No. 5 starter, which makes Arrighetti the No. 4. There’s no skipping him, but next time through, the Blue Jays may consider using an opener in front of Arrighetti.
2. The Adventures of Jesús Sánchez
How much longer can the Blue Jays run the risk of Jesús Sánchez roaming the outfield?

Sunday brought another glaring error when Sánchez dropped a simple fly ball in the second inning, which extended the inning for Arrighetti and cost him five more pitches. The odd blunder is excusable over 162 games, but these have become too common for Sánchez.

Out of 146 qualified outfielders, Sánchez is near the bottom with a -8 Fielding Run Value, metrically the weakest defender on a team that’s otherwise been among baseball’s best. This is actually a bit surprising for Sánchez, who had typically been closer to a league-average defender before being traded to the Blue Jays. This season, with a combination of physical and mental errors, it’s just not working.

The alternative is to have Myles Straw in left field, trading some offensive upside for much stronger defense and better speed. Given that the Blue Jays still profile as a lower-scoring team needing to win some tight games down the stretch, Straw makes a lot of sense in these spots. It could also leave the Blue Jays more willing to roll the dice on Sean Keys, who played just a handful of games in left field in Triple-A, but offers greater power upside than Sánchez and should be able to at least meet his 2026 standard defensively.
3. One bright spot: Josh Smith

Quietly, Smith has been one of the Blue Jays’ hottest hitters lately. His home run Sunday was his fourth in 18 games with the organization, too, a welcome sign in a lineup looking for a spark each night.
The Smith deal wasn’t the flashiest move of the Trade Deadline, coming over from the Rangers for lefty Adam Macko, but it’s working.

“When we acquired him, it was under the radar,” manager John Schneider said. “We still think he’s a good player who was having a down year. There are some things, mechanically, for him to get back to. He was aware of that, too. … He made some pretty quick adjustments.”

Immediately, Smith identified a disconnect between his upper and lower half. With that wrinkle smoothed out again, he’s unlocking better bat speed, and if he keeps hitting like this, he could force his way into the lineup more often down the stretch.

items.titleEn: Okamoto's career-high 4-hit night fuels Blue Jays' burst above .500
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- Can you believe it? The Blue Jays, just 19 games from the finish line, own the final postseason spot in the American League.

Saturday’s 4-3 win over the Royals moved the Blue Jays into a tie for the final AL Wild Card spot with the Guardians, but they hold that tiebreaker based on their head-to-head record this season (4-2).

The win also moved the Blue Jays to 72-71. Yes, the number on the left is finally bigger than the one on the right. For the first time since April 3, when the Blue Jays were 4-3, they’re back above .500.
“Feels like it’s been a while, but I love the way we’re playing,” manager John Schneider said. “Love the way we’re being resilient. We struck first, got punched back in the mouth and stayed on it.”
This is what mattered most:
1. Kazuma Okamoto: The complete package
This may have been the best night of Okamoto’s big league career, his first four-hit performance with two runs driven in.

Okamoto did it all, from his classics to some new material. There were two doubles, including one ripped just inches inside the third-base line, and that’s what we’re used to seeing from Okamoto. Everything he hits is hard, and just about everything he hits is yanked to the left side of the diamond. Oddly enough, though, Okamoto’s most impressive swing of the night may have been the sixth-inning single, which he shot out to right-center field, which is rare territory for the Japanese slugger.

Okamoto’s game is built on highs and lows. On one hand, he’s struck out 167 times, just three shy of the Blue Jays’ all-time franchise record shared by Jose Bautista (2017) and Matt Chapman (‘22). The trade-off has been Okamoto’s power, though, with 28 home runs.

“There have been some ups and downs,” Okamoto said through interpreter Yusuke Oshima. “I know my weaknesses, but I’m always working to make sure that I can hit the ones I’m having a hard time hitting.”

Okamoto cannot be turned into a contact hitter, and thankfully, the Blue Jays haven’t whispered that idea. They’ve let him lean into his incredible natural power, and while everyone involved understands that will come with some empty at-bats in between, Saturday showed us the next level of Okamoto. When he’s at his best, Okamoto isn’t just a complementary power bat, he can change games.
“We’ve come this far, so all we can do is win and hopefully go to the postseason,” Okamoto said. “That’s all we’re thinking about. Every game, we’re giving it our all.”
2. Max Scherzer keeps the fight alive

All the Blue Jays needed from Scherzer was “enough,” and that’s exactly what he gave them. Allowing just three runs over 5 2/3 innings, Scherzer kept the Blue Jays in the game just long enough and gave the bullpen just enough help -- another solid day from the 42-year-old.

“I feel great. My body’s really responding. I’m getting stronger every outing and I’m executing better,” Scherzer said. “Outside of the first inning, I felt like I did a pretty good job. Let’s keep this going. I feel healthy, I feel good, everything’s in a good spot. Keep it going.”

Scherzer’s late-season run is one of the best stories we’ve seen this season. Now past his thumb, forearm, ankle and back issues, Scherzer is helping keep this rotation together with Dylan Cease and José Soriano as the only other healthy, full-length starters.
From there? It’s scramble mode, but the Blue Jays don’t want to mess with Scherzer’s schedule.
“As of now, we’re trying to keep Max where he is and have him go after the [Thursday] off-day,” Schneider said. “We’ll cross that bridge after we get through tomorrow.”
3. The path forward: Going for the sweep
It’s scoreboard-watching season, and starter Spencer Arrighetti will try to lead the Blue Jays to a sweep against Randy Dobnak in Sunday's finale.

If you’re a Blue Jays fan, you’ll spend one more day pretending to be a Red Sox fan, where lefty Payton Tolle takes on the Orioles. The Blue Jays and Orioles still have six games against one another, so it’s important that the Blue Jays create a bit of a gap there to eliminate the risk of a run.
The Guardians, though, have Gavin Williams, who mowed down 13 Blue Jays batters this past Tuesday, so the AL Wild Card rival is positioned well against the Tigers.

items.titleEn: Taillon (right elbow inflammation) back on injured list
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- Jameson Taillon left Friday night’s start with right elbow discomfort, another setback just two innings into his first start back from the 15-day IL.

Taillon had been down with right forearm tendinitis, but he and the Blue Jays felt they’d caught that early, and he felt comfortable through a Triple-A rehab start before coming back to the big leagues. After just 29 pitches Friday night, though, John Schneider came out of the dugout to speak to the umpiring crew between innings while the bullpen quickly began to stir.
Taillon is now headed for an MRI after the Blue Jays’ 9-2 win over the Royals, and the club should have more information on Taillon this weekend.

“He said it felt a bit more nerve-y, if that makes sense,” John Schneider said. “He’s been through this a little bit and he said this felt a little bit different than the previous injury, so we’ll just see what the MRI says.”

This is a troubling blow to Taillon, the well-liked right-hander who is now in his 10th MLB season. After Taillon was designated for assignment by the Cubs just over a month ago, he was traded to the Blue Jays and immediately profiled as a rotation fill-in following the trade of Kevin Gausman. That hasn’t happened, though, and with so many injuries elsewhere in this rotation, the Blue Jays are back to scrambling.
Where does the rotation stand?

Dylan Cease is going to pitch every fifth day down the stretch, and with off-days each of the next three Thursdays, the Blue Jays can pull that off to maximize their ace’s value. The same could go for José Soriano, too, and if Max Scherzer feels strong, keep the trio rolling.

Beyond that, it’s messy. The Blue Jays have long been without José Berríos (Tommy John) and Cody Ponce (ACL). Even Bowden Francis (Tommy John) would have seen plenty of starts by now, but he was lost for the season. Shane Bieber is on the IL with right teres major inflammation, and Trey Yesavage underwent surgery to repair the meniscus in his left knee, but is chasing a comeback by the end of the regular season.

The result? Sunday’s finale against the Royals is already lined up as a bullpen day with Spencer Arrighetti as the “bulk guy”, either starting or following an opener. That was a fine enough plan for one spot in the rotation, but if the Blue Jays have two up in the air, this bullpen -- which is already running on fumes -- will be asked to carry the team.
The latest on Trey Yesavage
The Taillon news makes Yesavage’s timeline even more important.
The 23-year-old threw 23 pitches in a bullpen session Friday at the club’s complex in Dunedin, Fla., and felt fine. He was up to 92 mph in that session and is scheduled to throw another on Monday.

If all goes well, the Blue Jays would then get Yesavage on the mound facing some hitters at the complex on Thursday, simulating roughly two innings. It’s possible he pitches in a Minor League rehab game after that or continues to face hitters in a more controlled environment at the complex, but either way, it’s beginning to feel like Yesavage has a real shot to come back and help, even if he’d be pitching in shorter bursts.

items.titleEn: Blue Jays back to .500 and in thick of AL Wild Card race
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- Finally back to .500, the Blue Jays have 20 games to determine how we’ll remember the 2026 season and they’re playing their best baseball at exactly the right time.​

This isn’t the race the Blue Jays dreamed of when they entered the 2026 season as World Series contenders, fresh off taking the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7, but none of that matters now. The Blue Jays have given themselves another life, and with Friday’s 9-2 win over the Royals, are back to .500 (71-71). This leaves them just one game shy of the Guardians, who they hold a tiebreaker over.
“We’re gritty as hell,” said Ernie Clement. “If we go down early, we’re not afraid to come back. Right now, we’re punching first, which is something I don’t think we had done early in the season.”
This is what mattered most:
1. Another offensive outburst
This hasn’t been the Blue Jays’ “brand of baseball” by any means, but what a start Friday night.

With a flurry of blows right out of the gate, the Blue Jays hung four runs on the Royals in the first inning, capped by an Ernie Clement double into the left-field corner. This was a Clement classic, and much-needed after he’s been grinding through the past month offensively.

"The boys have done a great job picking me up after my historic month of August,” Clement joked. “These guys are awesome. We're playing great baseball. It’s not about me, so I’ve got to put my frustrations aside and try to help the team win. It felt good to get a couple, score a run, a couple of RBIs, just be part of a win.”

No one is going to mistake the 2026 Blue Jays for an offensive powerhouse, but with performances like this and the growing belief that Vladimir Guerrero Jr. could finally be turning a corner, there’s at least some optimism. Slowly and steadily, John Schneider has seen this grow since the Trade Deadline.

“Our at-bats have definitely been better and we’ve gotten some timely hitting,” Schneider said. “We got a lot of hits in the month of August as a team. We’re doing the little things better. We’re playing better defense. We’re keeping games where they should be better than we did at the beginning of the year. Then, the offense has kind of picked up a little bit.”
2. Key conversations around the Trade Deadline

The Blue Jays were trying to “thread the needle”. It’s so rare that teams actually pull that off, but with additions like José Soriano and the immediate impact of prospect returns like Brett Bateman, it’s working.

Leading up to that Deadline, Schneider and general manager Ross Atkins sought out players they knew would be sticking around and had some very direct, daily conversations with them. They wanted to get out in front of it.

“We really wanted to say that every day to the guys. ‘Hey, we still believe that a lot of you guys can be better and we’re just going to sell our entire [freaking] roster. We’re going to continue to compete,’” Schneider said. “I think that saying that every single day was important. Then, it was the guys believing that and going out and playing with it. That’s what we were trying to do.”
It’s taken some patience, but this is the vision the Blue Jays had all along.

“We’re a really good baseball team,” Clement said. “It was only a matter of time before things started clicking and we started playing our game, figured out our team identity, figured out our lineup. There’s been so many moving pieces throughout the whole year. It’s nice to finally have a solid grasp on who we are.”
3. The path forward

This weekend won’t get any easier for the Blue Jays after Jameson Taillon left Friday’s game following the second inning with right elbow discomfort. This bullpen, already running on fumes, needed to cover seven innings. There’s essentially another “bullpen day” around Spencer Arrighetti as the bulk guy on Sunday, too.

There can be no complaining from the driver’s seat, though. With the Guardians playing a motivated Tigers team, the Rangers playing the Rays and the Orioles playing the Red Sox, this weekend is wide open for the Blue Jays to separate themselves in the AL Wild Card race before some more winnable games against the A’s.

items.titleEn: All 30 teams set to open Spring Training 2027 on same day
bodyEn: Major League Baseball announced the 2027 Spring Training schedule on Friday.
All 30 MLB teams in Arizona’s Cactus League and Florida’s Grapefruit League will open Spring Training on Feb. 19.

Some of the first-day matchups include the Dodgers and White Sox facing off at their shared facility at Camelback Ranch in Glendale, Ariz., and the Yankees traveling to Dunedin, Fla., to play the Blue Jays.

As usual, the Spring Training schedule also features exhibition games at MLB parks. The Freeway Series will take place from March 21-23 -- the first game will be at Dodger Stadium on March 21 and the last two will be played at Angel Stadium.
Additionally, we’ll also see the Rays host the Blue Jays at Tropicana Field on March 20, as well as the Tigers on March 21 and 23.

The 2027 regular season will get underway on Wednesday, March 24, with an Opening Night game presented by Adobe, live on Netflix. That matchup will be announced at a later date. A day later, the traditional Opening Day presented by Adobe will feature 14 games, including a primetime matchup on NBC (the opponents for that game has yet to be determined).

items.titleEn: Cease's durability continues to define his dominant year
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- Dylan Cease is an overachiever. Somehow, after signing the biggest free-agent contract in the history of the Toronto Blue Jays, he’s exceeding expectations.

One year in, we’re already holding Cease’s 2026 season up against Cy Young winners of the past, from Roy Halladay’s peak seasons to Robbie Ray’s dominance in ‘21 and those two years of Roger Clemens, which live in a quiet corner of Blue Jays history but may never be topped.

That’s the ground Cease already stands on. If he’d given the Blue Jays an ERA just over 3.00 with some “wow” moments throughout the year, that would have been deemed a complete and total success, but he’s unlocked another level of himself. With six more scoreless innings in the Blue Jays' 11-0 victory Wednesday night in Cleveland, the biggest win of the Blue Jays’ season, Cease now owns a 2.25 ERA over 156 1/3 innings. He’s a workhorse starter with closer stuff. He’s a hitter’s nightmare who sticks around for the sixth and seventh innings.
That durability is the dividing line between good and great. Baseball is littered with hard throwers who stall out at 4 2/3 innings, but Cease has some old-school to him.

“I have a really good process,” Cease said. “I’m going from start to start and making little adjustments, then discussing with the group what I need to work on and where I can get better. I like my ability to execute right now, and even when I’m not at my sharpest, I can command my fastball enough to get outs. I like where I’m at.”
What’s a “process,” though? That word is intentionally mysterious.

In José Berríos’ peak seasons with the Blue Jays, which were built upon durability, we came to know the persona of “La Makina.” He was always working out, always lifting, always pushing his body to the limit. Cease, on the other hand, seems so much more laid-back. It almost tricks you into believing that this all comes naturally to him.

“It’s different, but it’s really consistent,” manager John Schneider said. “His throw days are consistent, his lift days are consistent and he does a lot of stuff behind the scenes in the weight room. You see it a little bit in his bullpen when he’s got his belts on, the stuff, the gadgets. He’s got a lot going on. He’s very meticulous with it, but not like the workout guru that José is.”
This is where Cease’s old-school approach to pitching meets the new age. Those gadgets, as Schneider calls them, may look a little odd at times, but they seem to be working.
“He’s very aware of all of that stuff. What’s Tom Brady’s thing, pliability?” Schneider said. “He’s very pliable. Dylan’s very aware of that stuff.”

Cease has topped 100 pitches in 16 of his 26 starts this season, which leads the Majors. Sure, part of that is the Tom Brady magic and some of it is a natural gift, but it’s also a mindset. Cease believes, fully and truly, that it’s his job to go seven-plus innings each time out. The bullpen is there to close out the game, not share the load with him equally.

This was new for Schneider and pitching coach Pete Walker, too, hearing Cease walk in the morning of a start -- or breeze by them between the third and fourth inning -- and grunt “I’ve got 120 in me today.” Who’s going to question him?

“He’s been doing this for a while, and he’s been durable for a while, so he has a good feel for it,” Schneider said. “I don’t want to just call him a liar out of the chute, either. I want him to prove himself right -- and he has, a lot of the time.”
Whether the hardware ultimately lands with Cease or the Yankees’ Cam Schlittler, this season is Cy Young caliber. That can’t be wasted, which has too often happened to this franchise.

From Pat Hentgen (1996) to Clemens (‘97-’98), Halladay (‘03) and Ray (‘21), the Blue Jays have never made the postseason in a year their pitcher has won the Cy Young Award. It takes more than just one star pitcher to achieve the ultimate goal, of course, but it’s a cruel coincidence.

Cease can win you a Wild Card game if you get him there. Get him to an ALCS or World Series, and he’s talented enough to steal you two. That still feels far away for these Blue Jays, but without Cease, it wouldn’t even be a conversation.

items.titleEn: King of the hill: Blue Jays' 20-year-old overpowering hitters as youngest pitcher on Double-A circuit
bodyEn: At an age when most pitchers are trying to establish themselves in the lower levels of the Minors, Johnny King is making one of the most difficult jumps in pro baseball look surprisingly easy.

Toronto’s No. 3 prospect has emerged as one of the organization’s biggest breakout stars in 2026, and the prized left-hander's recent promotion to Double-A New Hampshire has added another chapter to his rapid climb. Making his ascension all the more impressive is his age.
Get tickets to a Minor League game near you »

At just 20 years old, King is the youngest pitcher competing in the Eastern League, yet through his first four starts, he hasn't looked intimidated against opponents who, on average, are roughly five years his senior.

King delivered his latest statement on Wednesday night, equaling a season high with eight strikeouts over five scoreless innings for the Fisher Cats. King yielded three hits and a walk while generating an impressive 14 whiffs, keeping the opposition off the scoreboard for a second consecutive start.

Through his first four Eastern League starts, King sports a sparkling 1.50 ERA with 22 punchouts in 18 innings while holding opposing batters to a .136 average. Although his control has occasionally been an issue, his ability to miss bats has remained constant, and considering his age, the former is something the club expects will improve with experience.

But as impressive as his brief tenure with New Hampshire has been, it’s only been a continuation of an All-Star-caliber campaign. In 21 starts for High-A Vancouver, King posted a 3.21 ERA with a Northwest League-best 112 K’s in 84 innings.
And King's speedy movement through the system isn't new either.

Toronto selected the hurler in the third round of the 2024 Draft out of Naples, Florida. Just 17 at the time, King signed an above-slot deal worth $1.247,500 and entered the pro game as a high-upside project with enormous physical potential.

Long before he became one of the Blue Jays’ top pitching prospects, the 6-foot-3, 210-pounder was an outstanding all-around athlete. King was considered the best hitter on his high school team and possessed enough athletic ability that he could have potentially developed as a position player. But it was his left arm with consistent mid-90’s heat and a nasty curveball that ultimately captured Toronto’s interest.

King justified the choice to remain on the mound during his pro debut in 2025. The Michigan-born hurler posted a 2.48 ERA and fanned 105 in 61 2/3 innings across 18 appearances (15 starts) between Toronto's Rookie-level Florida Complex League squad and Single-A Dunedin.
Subscribe to the MLB Pipeline Newsletter

Now, barely two years removed from high school, King is no longer viewed as just a talented pitcher with potential. He’s a prospect who has quickly become one of Toronto’s most promising arms of the future -- and his breakout 2026 season suggests that's only for starters.

items.titleEn: Blue Jays secure tiebreaker with Guardians in tight AL Wild Card chase
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- The Blue Jays just took care of business in Cleveland and are now just a half-game out of the final American League Wild Card spot.
Thursday afternoon’s 6-3 win not only closes the gap in the Wild Card race, it also gives the Blue Jays a crucial tiebreaker over the Guardians in their head-to-head matchup (4-2) this season.
This is what mattered most:
1. The big picture
Never underestimate the value of a tiebreaker. Remember, the Yankees and Blue Jays both finished at 94-68 last season, but Toronto took the division crown courtesy of a tiebreaker.
Now that the Blue Jays hold that advantage over the Guardians, this is where it stands:
Blue Jays tiebreakers (full rules here):
Guardians: 4-2Orioles: 4-3 with six games remainingRangers: 0-4 with three games remaining (lost)Twins: 3-4Mariners: 4-2Tigers: 2-1 with three games remaining

The Guardians could quickly come back to life after an unimpressive week of baseball against the Blue Jays, but it’s beginning to feel more like the Orioles could be the biggest threat in this race when you consider their remaining games. The Blue Jays will host the Orioles at Rogers Centre from Sept. 11-13, then travel to Camden Yards for a three-game set Sept. 21-23.
2. Vladimir Guerrero Jr.? He’s still feeling it.

This wasn’t nearly as flashy as Vladdy’s performance on Wednesday, when he launched a three-run homer and finished with five RBIs. Guerrero was still as locked in as we’ve seen him in ages, though, even flipping his bat on a walk to open Toronto’s fourth inning after battling back from an 0-2 count.
In the fifth, Guerrero shot a sac fly out to right field and was pumping his right fist the moment he made contact, knowing he’d hit it deep enough to bring in Brett Bateman from third.

The Blue Jays need Guerrero to be their leader right now, and two days in a row, he’s shown the two ways that can be done. Every at-bat and every little run matters at this point in the AL Wild Card race, and if Guerrero is playing like that, the rest of this roster will follow.
3. Keys answers Schneider’s call
Asked recently what Sean Keys had to do to make his second stint in the big leagues more successful than the last, manager John Schneider had a quick, simple answer: “Hit breaking balls.”

Keys’ RBI single in the fourth came off a Tanner Bibbee sweeper at the bottom of the zone, an important swing that gives his manager more reason to trust him. It wasn’t a rocket off the bat -- not even close -- but Keys did well to hang back on the pitch instead of flying open too early in his swing.

This is all the Blue Jays need from Keys against good breaking pitches. If he can survive those and hunt fastballs, then his power can truly shine. He’s hit 29 home runs this season between Double-A, Triple-A and the big leagues, more than any other player in this organization. Toronto needs to steal a game or two down the stretch, and with this team so obviously lacking power, it’s going to be tempting to get Keys in there as often as possible.

items.titleEn: Yesavage to throw off mound Friday as part of late-season comeback plan
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- The Blue Jays need some heroes if they’re going to turn this forgettable season into one we remember, and Trey Yesavage is on the way.

Early in August, Yesavage underwent left knee surgery to repair his meniscus, but he’s scheduled to throw off a mound for the first time Friday at the Blue Jays’ complex in Dunedin, Fla. The 23-year-old has just over three weeks to get back by the end of the regular season, and in an AL Wild Card race that could be decided by a single game, that could make all the difference.
From here, this is what Yesavage’s ideal plan looks like:

1. The first bullpen -- When Yesavage throws off a mound Friday, the key will be how his knee responds the next day. This is Yesavage’s landing leg down the mound, so how will that respond to pitching closer to max effort?

2. Another bullpen -- If the first one goes well, the Blue Jays will need to see another. This one would likely come a few days later and could include a few more pitches, but will prove that Yesavage is ready to face hitters.
3. Live hitters -- This would likely be Yesavage facing some hitters down at the Blue Jays’ complex, close to max effort while simulating an inning or two.

4. Game action -- Keep in mind that the Triple-A Buffalo Bisons play their final game on Sept. 20. If Yesavage isn’t ready for this step by then, it could take the shape of a more formalized “sim game” at the complex, but he’s got a shot to line it up. Manager John Schneider says Yesavage would need “at least a game” to prove that he’s ready.
“If that goes well,” Schneider said, “we’ll see if he can help us out in some capacity.”

This schedule represents a perfect world for Toronto, but it’s what the club is hoping for. It’s difficult to put anything past Yesavage, either, who’s determined to get back if at all possible for another postseason run. If the Blue Jays fall out of this race by then, they are likelier to exercise extreme caution and back Yesavage off. But it looks like this will go down to the wire in late September.

Don’t expect Yesavage out there for six innings and 100 pitches, though. Instead, Toronto would be happy to see him build back up closer to half of his usual workload. Perhaps that lands him around three innings, four if he’s ultra efficient. The club is chasing his sheer upside at this point, not a grind-it-out start.

“That would make it interesting for a bullpen-y bulk day, with him being part of it,” Schneider said. “That would be nice. It just depends on how much time he’s missed, how much he can build up. Is it an inning or two? Is it three or four? We’ll cross that bridge when we get there.”

Schneider added that, if Yesavage comes back, it would be more tempting to just start Yesavage in the first inning, not using an opener, then figure out the bullpen from there. Most bulk relievers are pitchers caught between starting and relieving, but Yesavage would invent the “super bulk” role for the stretch run if this all works out, capable of filling a few innings with legitimately dominant upside.
So much still needs to go right between now and then, but Yesavage has a chance, and all the Blue Jays need is a chance.

items.titleEn: Ranking the 10 most impactful Trade Deadline moves, one month later
bodyEn: We all know who was the best player moved before this season's Trade Deadline. But now that we are one month clear of that date, has that player been the best midseason addition of the bunch?
Hint: No.
Tarik Skubal has been plenty good for the Dodgers, and you will find him in our ranking below of the top Deadline moves. But he's not No. 1. He's actually behind multiple other starting pitchers.
Here's a look at the top 10 most impactful Trade Deadline additions.
Notes: Limit one player per team. All stats updated through Tuesday unless noted otherwise.

1. Tyler Mahle, SP, BravesThe Braves were a Skubal suitor, but like every other club, they had to pivot after the jewel of the Deadline class was shipped to Los Angeles. Atlanta landed on the 31-year-old Mahle, who had a 5.13 ERA across 18 starts with the Giants and missed about a month of action earlier in the year due to a hamstring strain. Once the Deadline passed, he didn't even make it onto our list of the top 25 trades, but he has been everything the Braves could have wanted for their injury-ravaged rotation.

Mahle has allowed a total of five earned runs through his first five starts with the NL East leaders, spanning 30 1/3 innings. A greater reliance on his splitter has juiced Mahle's strikeout numbers and helped solve his issues against right-handed batters. His strikeout-minus-walk rate, which was a pedestrian 12.9% before the trade, is 23.1% since. And same-handed hitters have seen their OPS versus Mahle plummet from .848 to .583.

2. Clay Holmes, SP, CubsIn terms of total value, there is no doubt that the deal that brought Holmes to Chicago's North Side was the best one of Deadline season. Not only because he has been stellar for the Cubs, but because that swap with the Mets also included outfielder Tyrone Taylor, who owns a hefty .413/.462/.565 slash line through 52 plate appearances with Chicago.

Holmes hadn't pitched in about 10 weeks due to a fractured right leg when he was dealt to the Cubs. He stumbled a bit in his team debut, allowing four earned runs over four innings against the Royals on Aug. 8. But in four starts since then, he has given up one run in 25 innings.

3. Liam Hicks, C, RaysRays catchers finished 28th in wRC+ in 2024 and '25. They had been better this season ahead of the Deadline, but an offensive upgrade was still one of the club's top priorities. Enter Hicks, who perfectly fits the Rays' contact-heavy approach at the plate. But he's been doing a lot more than just putting the bat on the ball. He has been doing serious damage for the team with the best record in the American League.

Hicks, who has a .374 career slugging percentage through four Minor League seasons and had a .432 slug with the Marlins this year, is slugging .522 in 80 plate appearances with Tampa Bay. His .328 average, .425 on-base percentage and 163 wRC+ each rank inside the top 15 among the 195 hitters who have at least 80 PAs since Hicks first played for the Rays on Aug. 4.

4. Tarik Skubal, SP, DodgersHere's where Skubal slots in, and for just about any other pitcher, we'd be raving about his results with the Dodgers: a 3.00 ERA and an 11.1 K/9 rate over 30 innings (five starts). But for a reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner, Skubal's results draw more of a polite round of applause than a standing ovation. Still, he's looked really good his past few times out, including an 11-strikeout showing against the Pirates on Aug. 22. Skubal's FIP with the Dodgers is an impressive 2.29. That's third-best among qualified pitchers since August, trailing only the Rays' Drew Rasmussen (2.12) and the Reds' Chase Burns (2.17).

5. Luis García Jr., INF, YankeesIn no particular order, the Yankees' Trade Deadline priorities included bullpen help, a right-handed-hitting outfielder, another catcher and/or someone who could slot in at shortstop or third base.

And so, the Yanks' first headline add before the Deadline was ... a lefty-hitting infielder who plays on the right side of second base. However, García was still a huge get for a lineup that needed some pop. The 26-year-old has provided that, highlighted by a .511 slugging percentage, five home runs and 10 extra-base hits in his first 25 games with New York. He has multiple hits in four of his past eight games, including a four-hit night versus Houston on Aug. 25.
'Maybe the chain has power': Garcia's bat roaring with Yanks

6. Jo Adell, OF, GuardiansAcquiring left-hander Foster Griffin has been a plus for Cleveland, which can line him up behind the likes of ace Gavin Williams and standout rookie Parker Messick to form what could be a great rotation in a short playoff series. But what the Guardians really needed at the Deadline was more offensive firepower. Adell has brought that as he's posted 11 extra-base hits and an .815 OPS through 24 games.

Adell has been even better of late, slashing .327/.383/.527 over his previous 14 games. He enjoyed a six-RBI game in the middle of that stretch, something only one other Guardian (Angel Martínez) had achieved in the previous three calendar years. Prior to Adell's arrival, Cleveland ranked 27th in wRC+ (92). Since his first game on Aug. 4, they are tied for 11th in that stat (103).

7. Brett Bateman, OF, Blue JaysWhen the Blue Jays made the tough decision to trade away Kevin Gausman, they might have received their center fielder of the future in return. Bateman, Toronto's No. 16 prospect, made his MLB debut five days after the trade and has hit .317 with a .367 on-base percentage across 92 plate appearances since.

Speed and defense are considered his top tools, and those have definitely shown up in The Show. Bateman is 3-for-3 in steals through 20 games and has already racked up +3 outs above average during his short time in center.

8. Erik Miller, RP, Red SoxThe Red Sox made a huge splash on Deadline Day, grabbing catcher Adley Rutschman from the Orioles for five players, including three prospects. That deal hasn't yet worked out as Boston had hoped, but another move the club made on Aug. 3 has paid dividends. Miller, acquired from the Giants for former top prospect Marcelo Mayer, has absolutely dominated in a setup role in front of Aroldis Chapman, striking out 20 of the 46 batters he has faced. The lefty had thrown 10 1/3 scoreless innings before permitting a run during Monday's win over the Mariners. Most encouraging is the fact that Miller has walked only three batters in his 11 1/3 frames with Boston. He walked 22 batters in 32 2/3 innings with San Francisco before the trade.

9. Robbie Ray, SP, PadresSpeaking of walks, Ray has issued 16 in 26 1/3 innings with San Diego. But he has been able to work out of trouble often, as he has a 3.42 ERA through five starts. Ray indicated after his Aug. 18 start against the Mets that he has worked with Padres coaches to iron out some issues with his delivery, and when you include that evening's effort, the lefty has permitted only four earned runs through his past three outings (17 1/3 innings).

Ray has cut back on his four-seam fastball in favor of more changeups with the Padres. His usage on that pitch has increased 10 percentage points, up to 27%, and hitters have a .115 average (3-for-26) and a .448 OPS against it since he joined the NL Wild Card contenders.

10. Connor Norby, INF, RockiesNorby may be the only player in this top 10 who is not on a club with postseason hopes in 2026, but he is still worthy of inclusion after he reached base in each of his first 15 games with the Rockies after being acquired from the Marlins. The 26-year-old infielder has a .342 on-base percentage and seven extra-base hits through his first 21 games with Colorado. That includes Wednesday's walk-off victory over the Orioles, who drafted Norby in the second round in 2021.

He was once a high-ranking prospect in Baltimore's system but compiled an 89 wRC+ from 2024-26 with the Orioles and Marlins. Perhaps Norby will unlock his full potential while playing half of his games at the hitters haven that is Coors Field.

items.titleEn: Vladdy, Cease have Blue Jays looking their best in shutout win
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- Wednesday night felt like one long exhale at Progressive Field for the Blue Jays. For a few hours, everything went right.

Sure, the Guardians helped the Blue Jays along by extending some innings with ugly defensive play, but all you’ll remember is the 11-0 win and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. finally looking like himself, if only for a night.
The win moves the Blue Jays back within 1 1/2 games of the Guardians for the final AL Wild Card spot, leapfrogging the Orioles and Rangers, who both lost Wednesday.
This is what mattered most:
1. Glimpses of the old Vladimir Guerrero Jr.

Oh, what a night. Guerrero’s three-run shot was the star of the show, but on either side of that, Vladdy ripped an RBI double off the wall in left and shot an RBI single the other way to add on another run in the sixth.

"I think he was ready to hit a curveball and he hit a curveball,” said Guardians starter Joey Cantillo. “The second at-bat, same thing. He was ready to hit a curveball and he hit a curveball. We got him the third at-bat, which is good. But he's a good hitter, so when you leave pitches over the plate, he's going to hit."

It’s been so long since one of these games. Guerrero, at his best, can hold a game in the palm of his hand and control it completely, but we haven’t seen that since the Blue Jays’ 2025 postseason run. After the home run and later the RBI single, there were chants of “Vladdy” coming down from the Blue Jays fans in attendance, something else we haven’t heard in too long.
2. Same old Dylan Cease
No one deserved an easy night at the office more than Dylan Cease, who’s been stuck pitching in low-scoring deadlocks all season long.

“That’s nice because it definitely allows for a little more margin of error,” Cease said. “Ultimately, I try to pitch the same way, which is not to give up runs, obviously. Maybe it changes some pitch selections here and there, but ultimately, I still want to pitch pretty similarly.”

He still did the same old thing, though, cruising through the Guardians’ lineup over six innings of scoreless ball with four strikeouts. The outing dropped his ERA to 2.25, and in the AL Cy Young race against the Yankees’ Cam Schlittler, every start is going to matter down the stretch.

Cease has become a lock for six-plus innings. It’s such a rare combination in the modern game, when so many younger pitchers chase strikeouts but can’t match that with the durability and deep starts. Cease does both, and does it about as well as anyone.

“Dylan's been a really good strikeout pitcher his entire career. I think adding the changeup... He used to be just north-south -- heaters at the top, and then the two spin pitches underneath. And now he's pitching," Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said.
"You add pitching to that arsenal and that stuff, you're going to get what you're seeing. He's been dominant this year. He's been one of the best, if not the best, starters.”
The bonus? Cease did this on 83 pitches. The Blue Jays need him out there as often as possible down the stretch, and this sets it up beautifully.
“That helps. I’m assuming I’m going to be going [every] five [days] for a while, so any chance to do something like that strategically, it’s a good idea,” Cease said.
3. A playoff mentality

Once you’ve been through what the Blue Jays went through in 2025, right up to Game 7 of the World Series against the Dodgers, “stress” takes on a different definition. In theory, a race for the third Wild Card spot should be much more manageable.
All of the “extras” can’t possibly compare, because there’s not the same media circus filling every empty second of manager John Schneider’s day, but there’s a mindset they can still reach back for.

“The mentality, going back to that Seattle series [in the ALCS] when we were coming home down 3-2,” Schneider said, “we just had to win tomorrow. We had to win the next day and figure it out. That’s the mentality right now.”

After Game 5 in Seattle, Ernie Clement sat at his locker, calm and cool, and said the Blue Jays were right where they wanted to be, controlling their own destiny even if they were down in the series. That’s the same mentality they need to carry through the final 22 games.

items.titleEn: Could this swing mark the return of vintage Vladdy?
bodyEn: CLEVELAND -- Months ago, in the early days of Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s season-long struggles, he said he wouldn’t feel like he’s truly “back” until he could stand at home plate and watch his own home run fly. Only then could he really feel it.
The moment Guerrero made contact Wednesday night in Cleveland, he didn’t move an inch.

The towering, three-run shot soared to right field, a no-doubter from the moment Guerrero made contact. He strolled across the plate, in awe of what he’d done, and flipped his bat to the ground as the ball crashed into the bleachers. He hadn’t even left the dirt yet, hadn’t taken a single step down the first-base line.
Chants of “Vladdy! Vladdy! Vladdy!” rained down from the Blue Jays fans who had packed the bleachers above the Blue Jays’ dugout.

This is what it’s supposed to look like, and this is what we’ve spent all season waiting to see. On his first at-bat of the game, Guerrero made an excellent adjustment and drove a breaking ball off the left-field wall for an RBI double. Then, on the home run swing, his body exploded through the ball, the dozens of moving pieces finally coming together to play the right notes at the right time. We haven’t heard that song in ages.

This is only Guerrero’s eighth home run of the season, and he still doesn’t have one at Rogers Centre, but any flicker of hope is worth grabbing onto at this point. The Blue Jays are chasing the third AL Wild Card spot, which has been dancing just out of their grasp for too long, but Guerrero is the shortcut. Without Guerrero, the Blue Jays need to play their best baseball of the season in every possible way for the next three-plus weeks. If Guerrero suddenly comes back to life, though, that’s a rocket strapped to this ball team’s back.

At the same time, the Blue Jays -- and their fans, who have watched with frustration all summer -- have learned to be wary of false hope. Guerrero, his manager and his teammates have repeatedly said that when it comes, it will click in an instant and Guerrero will catch fire. His first seven home runs this season didn’t turn a spark into a flame, though, so why will this one?

All the Blue Jays have is the hope that it will, but that’s enough for now. The player that lit the 2025 postseason on fire hasn’t gone anywhere and certainly hasn’t disappeared, Guerrero has just been completely unable to find that version of himself in 2026. If he can find that again, or even a sliver of that player, it can help fuel a postseason run that would completely change how we view Guerrero’s 2026 season.
One more time we’re left to wonder: What if this is the swing? What if Vladdy’s found it?
